title: Wave Motion
short_intro: Wave motion refers to the propagation of disturbances transferring energy and momentum through a medium or vacuum without bulk transport of matter. It is mathematically characterized by space-time periodic functions obeying the linear wave equation.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definitions of transverse and longitudinal waves, relation between wave velocity, frequency, and wavelength (v = fλ), particle velocity versus wave velocity, reflection of waves, and stationary waves.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Differential wave equation in 1D and 3D, phase velocity, group velocity, energy density and intensity of wave motion, acoustic impedance, and Doppler effect in sound.

concept_notes.heading: Kinematics of Progressive Waves
bullets: A progressive wave travels continuously in a given direction without attenuation in an ideal medium.
The displacement y(x,t) of a particle at position x and time t for a sinusoidal wave is given by y(x,t) = A sin(kx - ωt + φ).
The phase difference Δφ between two points separated by distance Δx is given by Δφ = kΔx = (2π/λ)Δx.

concept_notes.heading: Particle Velocity vs Wave Velocity
bullets: Wave velocity (v) is the speed at which the phase of the wave propagates through the medium, given by v = fλ = ω/k.
Particle velocity (u) is the instantaneous velocity of a medium particle executing SHM, given by u = ∂y/∂t = -ωA cos(kx - ωt + φ).
The maximum particle velocity is u_max = ωA, which is distinct from the wave velocity v.

concept_notes.heading: Energy and Intensity in Wave Motion
bullets: A wave element of mass dm = ρ dx possesses kinetic and potential energy as it oscillates.
The average energy density E (energy per unit volume) of a sinusoidal wave is E = 2π^2 f^2 A^2 ρ = (1/2)ρω^2 A^2.
Intensity (I) is the average power transmitted per unit area perpendicular to the wave propagation direction, given by I = Ev = (1/2)ρω^2 A^2 v.

concept_notes.heading: Reflection and Boundary Conditions
bullets: Reflection from a rigid (fixed) boundary introduces a phase change of π (or 180°) and a sign inversion in the reflected displacement wave.
Reflection from a free (open) boundary occurs with zero phase change, meaning the reflected displacement wave is in phase with the incident wave.
Superposition of incident and reflected waves of equal amplitude forms standing (stationary) waves with distinct nodes and antinodes.

derivations.title: One-Dimensional Classical Wave Equation
derivations.conditions: Ideal, linear, homogeneous elastic medium obeying Newton's second law.
steps: Consider a small string element of length dx and linear mass density μ. The tension at x is T and at x+dx is T + (∂T/∂x)dx.
Applying Newton's second law to the vertical transverse motion: (μ dx)(∂^2 y / ∂t^2) = (T + (∂T/∂x)dx) sin(θ + dθ) - T sin(θ).
For small angles, sin(θ) ≈ tan(θ) = ∂y/∂x, and assuming uniform tension T, the vertical force simplifies to T (∂^2 y / ∂x^2) dx.
Equating inertial force to restoring force: μ dx (∂^2 y / ∂t^2) = T (∂^2 y / ∂x^2) dx.
derivations.result: \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = \frac{T}{\mu} \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2} = v^2 \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}

derivations.title: Relation Between Phase Velocity and Group Velocity
derivations.conditions: Dispersive medium where phase velocity v depends on angular frequency ω or wave number k.
steps: Define phase velocity as v_p = \omega / k and group velocity as v_g = d\omega / dk.
Express angular frequency as \omega = k v_p(k).
Differentiate with respect to k: v_g = \frac{d}{dk}(k v_p) = v_p + k \frac{dv_p}{dk}.
Using wavelength λ = 2\pi / k, rewrite the derivative in terms of λ to obtain the standard dispersive form.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement-Distance (y-x) Snapshot Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sinusoidal wave curve plotted with displacement y on the vertical axis and position x on the horizontal axis at a fixed time t.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the spatial profile of the wave at one instant. The horizontal distance between successive crests represents the wavelength (λ).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested for identifying wavelength, amplitude, and spatial phase relationships.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement-Time (y-t) History Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sinusoidal curve plotted with displacement y on the vertical axis and time t on the horizontal axis for a fixed position x.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the temporal oscillation of a specific particle in the medium. The time period (T) corresponds to the interval between successive identical phase states.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to determine particle frequency, time period, and instantaneous particle velocity (∂y/∂t).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Melde's Experiment Apparatus
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A taut string connected to an electrically driven tuning fork, passing over a pulley to a pan holding variable masses (tension adjustment).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the formation of transverse stationary waves and verifies the relation between wave frequency, tension, and linear mass density (v = √(T/μ)).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on transverse stationary wave modes (p-loops) under parallel and perpendicular tuning fork configurations.

solved_numericals.question: A progressive wave is represented by y = 0.05 sin(100πt - 2πx), where x and y are in meters and t in seconds. Find the frequency and wavelength of the wave.
solution_steps: Compare the given equation y = 0.05 sin(100πt - 2πx) with the standard wave equation y = A sin(ωt - kx).
Identify angular frequency ω = 100π rad/s and wave number k = 2π rad/m.

solved_numericals.question: The tension in a stretched string is increased by 21%. If the mass per unit length remains constant, calculate the percentage increase in the wave velocity.
solution_steps: The velocity of a transverse wave in a string is given by v = √(T / μ).
Taking natural logarithms: ln v = (1/2) ln T - (1/2) ln μ.
Differentiating for small fractional changes: Δv / v = (1/2)(ΔT / T).
Given ΔT / T = 0.21, substitute this into the relation: Δv / v = (1/2) × 21% = 10.5%.

solved_numericals.question: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels in air with a velocity of 340 m/s. What is the phase difference between two points on the wave separated by a distance of 34 cm?
solution_steps: Calculate the wavelength using λ = v / f = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m = 68 cm.
Substitute the given path difference Δx = 34 cm and λ = 68 cm: Δφ = (2π / 68) × 34.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: The amplitude of oscillation is infinitesimally small compared to the wavelength, ensuring the linear approximation (sin θ ≈ tan θ) holds true.
Limitation: Nonlinear wave effects (such as shock wave formation and harmonic distortion) are neglected in the standard linear wave equation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Particle velocity and wave velocity are the same physical quantity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Particle velocity is the periodic velocity of a medium particle in SHM, whereas wave velocity is the speed at which the wave profile propagates.
common_misconceptions.why: Particle velocity depends on time and position within the wave cycle (maximum at equilibrium), while wave velocity is a constant property determined by the elastic and inertial properties of the medium.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Energy travels along with the individual particles in a progressive wave.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only energy and momentum are transported forward; the medium particles only oscillate about their equilibrium mean positions.
common_misconceptions.why: Wave motion is a collective disturbance propagation without net displacement of matter.

quick_revision: Wave velocity depends strictly on medium properties (v = √(T/μ) or v = √(γP/ρ)), whereas frequency depends solely on the source.
Progressive Wave Equation: y(x,t) = A \sin(kx - \omega t)
